Paper Content:
Controlling dynamics of stochastic systems with deep reinforcement learning
Ruslan I. Mukhamadiarov
Arnold Sommerfeld Center for Theoretical Physics and Center for NanoScience, Department of Physics,
Ludwig-Maximilians-Universit¨at M¨unchen, Theresienstrasse 37, D-80333 Munich, Germany
A properly designed controller can help improve the quality of experimental measurements or
force a dynamical system to follow a completely new time-evolution path. Recent developments in
deep reinforcement learning have made steep advances toward designing effective control schemes
for fairly complex systems. However, a general simulation scheme that employs deep reinforcement
learning for exerting control in stochastic systems is yet to be established. In this paper, we attempt
to further bridge a gap between control theory and deep reinforcement learning by proposing a
simulation algorithm that allows achieving control of the dynamics of stochastic systems through
the use of trained artificial neural networks.
Specifically, we use agent-based simulations where
the neural network plays the role of the controller that drives local state-to-state transitions. We
demonstrate the workflow and the effectiveness of the proposed control methods by considering
the following two stochastic processes: particle coalescence on a lattice and a totally asymmetric
exclusion process.
I.
INTRODUCTION
Gaps in theoretical knowledge can seriously compromise the control efforts since control application relies on
dynamical equations that describe the time evolution of
the system [1, 2]. At the same time, a variety of dynamic
aspects of a system can be learned when trying to exert
control over it. A representative example of how theory
and control can benefit from each other is aerospace exploration, where the successful design of propulsion, guidance, and landing control systems was accomplished after failure-driven improvements in understanding of aerodynamics, combustion, high-pressure physics, and other
fields of science.
Furthermore, application of control
techniques can drastically increase the performance of experimental setups that use feedback loops [3], e.g., atomic
force microscope (AFM) [4–6], and with this open new
doors for cutting-edge scientific exploration.
The central goal of control theory is to design a control scheme
or a controller that is capable of altering the dynamics
of the system or driving state-to-state transitions in an
effective manner [7]. These tasks are achieved by choosing control setups that minimize the error between the
controller’s output and the desired signal. A typical controller consists of feed-forward, feedback elements, PID
(proportional-integral-derivative) controllers, or cascades
of these elements. If equations that describe the dynamics of the system are known, one of the most efficient
ways to instill a control law on a system is to use established methods from the optimal control, which tune the
controller parameters and then evaluate the controller’s
performance through a certain index, e.g., action, thermodynamic potential, survivability [8, 9].
In practice, the ability of a controller to fulfill its purpose may be seriously impacted by incomplete knowledge
of the system’s dynamics and by uncertainties that are
not directly accounted for by the dynamical model of
the system. The latter often comes from environmental
disturbances, aging of system components, or statistical noise (e.g., from sensor readings) and can be tackled by minimizing the mean squared error between predicted and observed internal states with the help of the
Kalman filter and its variations [10, 11]. As for explicitly
missing information, robust control methods have been
developed to account for the gaps in the knowledge by
minimizing the error between partially known and the
“true” dynamics of the system [12, 13]. Other fairly recent approaches that attempt to learn about the system’s
dynamics and reduce the uncertainties while simultaneously exerting control over it are adaptive control and
reinforcement learning [14–17].
A serious limitation of the methods mentioned above is
a prohibiting number of equations and their control parameters, which need to be optimized to achieve control
over complex systems. However, with the rising popularity of machine learning and the realization that feedforward neural networks can serve as universal approximators [18], a new powerful approach that is called deep
reinforcement learning gained considerable attention in
the scientific community [19, 20].
The approach combines the use of neural networks and concepts that have
already been developed from reinforcement learning that
enable efficient learning of the system dynamics through
interactions of the agent with the environment. To mention some of its applications, in statistical mechanics of
non-equilibrium systems, deep reinforcement learning is
used for exerting control on epidemic systems [21, 22],
for studying the problem of urban traffic [23], and for
studying cooperation dynamics of predator-prey models
[24, 25]. In biophysics, reinforcement learning has been
used to devise efficient navigation strategies [26–29] and
state-to-state transition protocols for active matter [30],
for finding optimal self-assembly protocols [31], and for
studying communicating matter [32, 33] and smart microswimmers [34, 35].
In quantum systems, reinforcement learning has been used to enhance quantum control
techniques [36], to improve the performance of quantum
simulations [37], and to optimize quantum variational
circuits [38]. Outside of physics, reinforcement learning
is best known for finding efficient game strategies that

outperform world champions [39, 40], for training robots
[41, 42], language recognition models [43, 44], computer
vision models [45, 46], etc.
Deep reinforcement learning has brought us closer to
a control engineer’s dream, where one states a desire,
turns on the controller, and lets the controller figure out
what to do [3]. However, it is still not clear whether the
deep reinforcement learning method can be successfully
applied to control multi-agent stochastic systems. Would
a targeted control be at all effective on a microscopic scale
in the presence of random forces, and to what degree
must the underlying dynamics of stochastic systems be
changed for a controller to achieve specific objectives?
In this work, we investigate these questions by proposing a new simulation method that controls the dynamics
of stochastic systems with the help of deep reinforcement
learning. The idea behind the method is to use artificial
neural networks as a controller that computes transition
probabilities between different local states for individually selected agents. In order to test the effectiveness of
our control method, we simulate the stochastic dynamics
of two different processes on a regular lattice – the particle coalescence and the driven particle transport with
exclusion. We find that replacing the original reaction
scheme with a neural network controller that reshapes
transition probabilities is reminiscent of developing new
interparticle interactions that help to achieve the desired
dynamical behavior.
At the same time, by the design
of our simulation method, sequentially selecting random
agents for the update in multi-particle systems undermines the effectiveness of the control measures since the
agents cannot react to the ever-changing environment until they are picked again for the update. Finally, we were
able to achieve more complex control objectives by employing a compound reward structure, as we show in our
studies of the heterogeneous traffic problem.

Similarly to looking for a control law that optimizes the

transition probability p(s′, r|s, a), where s′ is the next
state, then finding the optimal policy comes down to solving Bellman optimality equations [47]. However, finding
a control law for a system with known dynamics can also
be done with other well-developed methods from control
theory, such as optimal control.
One of the key strengths of the reinforcement learning
method is its ability to find optimal solutions to the control problem when we know nothing about the rules that
prescribe the system’s evolution. For these scenarios, one
can collect the state transition experiences, record them
into {s, a, r, s′} table, and then use the bootstrapping
methods to approximate the optimal policy [48, 49]. The
downside of such an approach is the inoperable size of the
experience tables and huge sets of coupled Bellman equations that result from these tables, which, until recently,
severely encumbered practical applications of reinforcement learning to large-scale systems [16]. Only after substantial advances in machine learning did it become possible to apply the ideas from reinforcement learning for
large systems by replacing the need to solve innumerable sets of equations with a neural network parameter
optimization procedure.

be controlled with deep reinforcement learning, we introduce the agent-based simulation method, which is
a combination of a familiar random sequential update
scheme and a trained neural network that drives local
state transitions. In contrast to typical stochastic simulations where the system’s dynamics is specified by hardcoded transition rates, the transition rates in our method
are determined by an artificial neural network. As it is

output as Q(s, a) values that are then converted to transitional probabilities P(a|s). However, before the neural
network can do such mapping and fulfill desired control
objectives, it needs to be trained first.

At the post-training phase, the network parameters become fixed, and the transition probabilities are fixed as well. The agents then follow these transition probabilities to update their states in the simulation. The way the transition probabilities are implemented in the simulation is by choosing, for each agent, a neighboring site (if available) and offering the action a with probability P(a|s). The selected agent then attempts to move to the neighboring site, provided that the movement is allowed by the transition probability. If the transition is allowed, the action a is executed, and the neighboring site is updated accordingly. If not, the agent remains at the same site, and the process continues.

Finally, we have to mention that the choice of using feed-forward neural networks is not the only option that we considered. We also explored the use of recurrent neural networks, but we found that the feed-forward networks provided sufficient flexibility for the purposes of this work, and they also allowed for more straightforward implementation and training.

In the next section, we will outline the specific simulation architecture that we used for the two selected stochastic processes.

 Arch iecture
 We begin by detailing the simulation architecture that we have developed for the two selected stochastic processes. For each of the processes, we have a different state representation, a different set of actions that the agent can perform, and different transition rules that describe how the state of the system evolves in response to the actions taken by the agents. Since both processes are defined on a regular lattice, we will describe the lattice-based architecture that we have used to implement them.

For the first process, we consider a particle coalescence on a regular lattice. The state of the system is described by the positions of all the particles on the lattice. Each site of the lattice can be either occupied by a particle or empty. The action that an agent can perform is to move to a neighboring site, provided that the site is empty, or to stay at the same site. The transition probability depends on the current state of the system and the action that the agent takes. In this case, the transition probability is determined by the Q(s, a) values output by the neural network, which are then used to compute the P(a|s) probabilities via the Softmax function (Eq. 4). The neural network takes as input the state s, which is the current configuration of particles on the lattice, and outputs Q-values for each possible action a that the agent can take. The actions available to the agent are moving to the left, moving to the right, or staying in place. Each of these actions has a corresponding Q-value, which is then passed through the Softmax function to produce the transition probabilities. Once the transition probabilities are determined, the agent chooses an action based on these probabilities and updates the system accordingly. If the chosen action is moving to an occupied site, the agent cannot move, and the transition probability for that action is zero. If the chosen action is moving to an empty site, the agent moves there, and the transition probability for that action is set to one. If the chosen action is staying in place, the agent remains at the same site, and the transition probability for that action is set to zero. This way, the neural network determines the transition probabilities for each action, and the system evolves according to these probabilities.
